title: Guaranteed Income Supplement
subtitle: Keep the income-tested benefit from becoming a July mystery

blocks.text: July is a lovely month for patios and a surprisingly ambitious month for government recalculations. If a Guaranteed Income Supplement changes, the tax return is usually somewhere in the plot.

GIS is a monthly, tax-free benefit for people 65 or older with low income who get the Old Age Security pension and live in Canada. It is worked out again each year from your income and marital status, usually using last year’s tax return. It is paid with OAS in one deposit.

For July to September 2026, a single, widowed or divorced person with yearly income below $22,800 may get up to $1,123.17 a month. That top amount is not a personal quote, and it changes every three months.

items.title: “GIS is simply a larger version of OAS.”
items.text: OAS is a taxable pension based on how long you have lived in Canada. GIS is a tax-free top-up, based on income, for OAS recipients who live here. They share a deposit, not a personality.

blocks.text: Service Canada: GIS overview
Knowing what the July review checks keeps a smaller deposit from catching you off guard.
blocks.detail: Your household type, last year’s tax return and any change in your income all shape the number.
blocks.extra: Section 02 shows which income limit fits your household.

sections.title: One Income Limit Does Not Fit Every Household

blocks.text: To qualify, you usually must be at least 65, get OAS, live in Canada, not be under a sponsorship agreement and have income below the limit for your household. A spouse or common-law partner’s income and benefits also shape the amount.

items.title: SINGLE, WIDOWED OR DIVORCED
items.text: Yearly income below $22,800. Top monthly GIS of $1,123.17.

items.title: PARTNER GETS FULL OAS
items.text: Combined yearly income below $30,096. Top monthly GIS for the recipient is $676.09.

items.title: PARTNER GETS THE ALLOWANCE
items.text: Combined yearly income below $42,144. Published top monthly GIS is $676.09.

items.title: PARTNER GETS NEITHER
items.text: Combined yearly income below $54,624. Top monthly GIS is $1,123.17.

blocks.text: OAS itself is left out of the income limits in the GIS rate tables. CPP, workplace pensions, RRSP withdrawals and investment income can all change the amount.
The earnings exemption usually protects the first $5,000 of job or self-employment income, plus half of earnings between $5,000 and $15,000.

items.title: “If two seniors receive the same OAS, they should receive the same GIS.”
items.text: GIS depends on income, marital status and what benefits a partner gets. Matching OAS deposits do not turn two households into matching tax returns.

blocks.text: Service Canada: GIS amounts

sections.title: File Before July Comes Looking for Answers

blocks.text: Service Canada reviews GIS each July using last year’s federal tax return. If you file the return on time, you are usually renewed on your own. The July letter may renew, change, stop or restart the benefit, or ask for more income details.

Both partners should file a return on time every year. A return with zero income still gives the government the family details it needs for income-based benefits. Blank income and missing information are not the same thing.

If your income dropped because you retired or a pension stopped or fell, Service Canada may estimate this year’s income instead of using last year’s higher amount. Contact Service Canada and send the Statement of Income it asks for.

GIS may stop if you are away from Canada for more than six months, unless you qualify to keep getting it. Tell Service Canada before you leave and after you come back so you are less likely to be overpaid.

items.title: “Once GIS starts, it renews forever without further action.”
items.text: GIS is checked every year. A late return, a change in income, marital status or where you live, or missing information can change or pause your payment. GIS is renewable, not immortal.

blocks.text: Key takeaway
File every year, read the July letter, report changes to your marital status or where you live, and contact Service Canada when your retirement income drops.

sections.title: Bernard and the Pension That Retired Twice

blocks.text: Meet Bernard
paragraphs: Bernard LeBlanc lives in Bathurst. He stops working in February, and his workplace pension drops later that spring. His goal is simple. He wants his budget to cover rent, groceries and the heat bill through the winter.

In July, his GIS letter arrives. The amount is far lower than he planned. The letter used last year’s income, back when he had a paycheque. Bernard decides his retirement has somehow retired twice while his bills stay impressively employed.

He reads it again. Rent is due in two weeks. A neighbour tells him not to bother, because “they just use your taxes and that’s that.” Bernard nearly believes it. Waiting a year for his next tax return feels like the only choice.

Then he finds one line near the bottom. If your income dropped this year, you can contact Service Canada. Bernard decides to call instead of wait. He knows a strongly worded glance at the letter will not change anything.

He gathers his pension statement, his last pay slip and his wife’s income details. Service Canada asks for a Statement of Income. He fills it in that week and keeps the confirmation number on the fridge.
There is one more surprise. His wife has not filed her return, and GIS needs both. She files it right away.
A few weeks later, his file is reviewed again. The new amount uses this year’s lower income. Bernard pays the rent on time. His retirement now retires only once, which he feels is the correct number.

blocks.text: When a July amount looks wrong, check the tax year used, your marital status, your partner’s benefit and your income sources before you ask for a review.
Bernard got his GIS reworked by sending his real income this year instead of waiting a year.
blocks.detail: If your income drops after you retire, the same Statement of Income can bring your payment in line with your life now.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

items.title: What five conditions belong in a GIS check?
items.detail: You are usually at least 65, get OAS, live in Canada, are not under a sponsorship agreement and have income below the limit for your household.

items.title: Why can two OAS recipients receive different GIS amounts?
items.detail: GIS depends on income, marital status and what benefits a partner gets.

items.title: What usually happens each July?
items.detail: Service Canada reviews GIS using last year’s federal tax return. It may renew, change, stop or restart the benefit, or ask for information.

items.title: How is work income treated differently?
items.detail: The earnings exemption usually protects the first $5,000, plus half of earnings between $5,000 and $15,000.

items.title: What should you do after a big drop in retirement income?
items.detail: Contact Service Canada and send the Statement of Income it asks for, so this year’s income can be estimated.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): GIS July Renewal and Income Change File

blocks.text: Use rounded numbers and short labels. Do not write your SIN, bank details or full pension account numbers here.
GIS is added to OAS as one payment. Use your letter, not the bank deposit total alone, to see how much comes from each benefit.

items.title: GIS
items.text: Guaranteed Income Supplement. A tax-free top-up for OAS recipients with low income.

items.title: Income-tested
items.text: The amount changes based on set income rules.

items.title: Combined income
items.text: The income of both spouses or common-law partners that counts.

items.title: Earnings exemption
items.text: Work income that GIS does not fully count.

items.title: Annual review
items.text: The July recheck using last year’s information.

items.title: Statement of Income
items.text: A form Service Canada may ask for to estimate this year’s income.

items.title: Overpayment
items.text: Money paid above what you were owed, which you may have to pay back.

quiz.question: True or False: “GIS is simply a larger version of OAS.”

questions: Are you 65 or older and getting OAS? (Yes / Not yet / Not sure)
Are you single, widowed or divorced, or do you have a spouse or partner? If you have a partner, do they get OAS, the Allowance or neither?
About what was your household income last year, not counting OAS? An estimate is fine.
Did your income drop this year because you retired or a pension changed? (Yes / No / Not sure)
Have you, and your partner if you have one, filed last year’s tax return? (Yes / No / Not sure)
What is one thing you will check or send before the next July review?
samples: Married. My wife gets full OAS.
Yes. I stopped working in February.
I filed. My wife has not yet.
Send Service Canada a Statement of Income.
